lessons.title: Spot, Forward and Futures Rates: Why the Forward Premium Exists

children.text: Suresh runs a garment export unit in Tiruppur. His US buyer will pay him $200,000 in three months. Spot USD/INR is 95.50, but when he asks his bank to lock a rate for three months from now, the bank offers him about 96.19, not 95.50. On NSE, the near-month USD/INR futures contract is also trading above spot. Is the bank predicting the rupee will fall? No. The gap is almost entirely arithmetic, and once you see the arithmetic, you will never mistake a forward rate for a forecast again.

body.text: A forward rate is not a prediction. It is today's spot rate adjusted for the interest rate gap between two currencies. Because Indian interest rates are higher than US rates, the dollar costs more for future delivery than it does today.

children.text: Three Prices for the Same Dollar

markDefs.definition: The rate for exchanging currencies now, with settlement in two business days. It is the standard headline quote.
A private contract, usually with a bank, to exchange a fixed amount of currency on a fixed future date at a rate agreed today.
A standardised, exchange-traded contract to buy or sell currency at a set price on a future date, cleared by the exchange's clearing corporation.

children.text: Why the Future Dollar Costs More

Imagine a bank offered to sell dollars one year forward at today's spot rate of 95.50. Anyone who needs dollars in a year now has two choices. They can convert rupees to dollars today and earn the lower US interest rate for a year. Or they can keep the rupees in India, earn the higher Indian rate for a year, and buy the dollars forward at 95.50. The second route gives the same dollars at the same exchange rate plus more interest, so everyone would choose it. Banks quoting that forward would lose money on every deal. To remove the free lunch, the forward rate must rise until the extra interest on rupees is exactly cancelled out. That gap is the forward premium.

body.latex: F = S \times \frac{1 + r_{INR} \times t}{1 + r_{USD} \times t}
body.caption: F = forward rate, S = spot rate, r = annual interest rate for each currency, t = time in years. This is covered interest rate parity.

children.text: Worked example with illustrative one-year market rates: rupee rate 6.50%, dollar rate 3.60%, spot 95.50. F = 95.50 × 1.065 ÷ 1.036 = 98.17. The forward premium is 98.17 minus 95.50 = ₹2.67, or 2.80% of spot for one year. That is almost exactly the 2.90 percentage point gap between the two interest rates.

body.title: Show me why this has to hold: the two paths

children.text: Start with ₹95,50,000 and one year to invest it. Both paths below are risk-free, so they must end with the same number of rupees. If they did not, banks would pile into the better one until prices adjusted.

content.caption: Two risk-free ways to invest ₹95,50,000 for one year (illustrative rates)
headers: Path B: go into dollars and lock the way back

cells: Sell $103,600 at the forward rate F, agreed today

children.text: If the bank quoted a forward below 98.17, Path A would win, and dealers would sell rupees forward until the rate rose. If it quoted above 98.17, Path B would win and the reverse would happen. Arbitrage pins the forward to the interest rate gap.

body.label: Quick rule of thumb
body.value: Annual forward premium ≈ Indian interest rate minus US interest rate
body.context: The exact formula gives a slightly smaller number, but for quick checks the rate gap is close enough. Real market premiums also shift with dollar demand, RBI actions and hedging flows.

body.title: Price a one-year forward
body.prompt: Spot USD/INR is 95.50. The one-year rupee interest rate is 6.00% and the one-year dollar rate is 3.75%. Using F = S × (1 + r_INR) ÷ (1 + r_USD), what is the one-year forward rate? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: F = 95.50 × 1.06 ÷ 1.0375 = 101.23 ÷ 1.0375 = 97.57. The premium is ₹2.07, or 2.17% of spot, close to the 2.25 percentage point rate gap. A narrower interest rate gap means a smaller forward premium.

children.text: Reading Forward Quotes: Points and Annualised Premium

markDefs.definition: The difference between the forward rate and the spot rate, quoted in paise for USD/INR. Added to spot when the forward is at a premium.
The forward premium expressed as a yearly percentage of spot, so forwards of different tenors can be compared.

children.text: Dealers do not quote the full forward rate. They quote
forward points
, the paise to add to spot. Newspapers and RBI data go one step further and convert the premium into an
annualised premium
, so a 3-month and a 1-year forward can be compared on equal terms.

body.caption: Converts any forward premium into a yearly percentage
An illustrative USD/INR forward curve (spot 95.50, rupee rate 6.50%, dollar rate 3.60%)

body.title: Annualise the premium
body.prompt: Spot USD/INR is 95.50 and a bank quotes the 3-month forward at 96.20. What is the annualised forward premium, in percent? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Premium = 96.20 minus 95.50 = ₹0.70. As a share of spot: 0.70 ÷ 95.50 = 0.733%. Annualise by multiplying by 12 ÷ 3 = 4: 0.733% × 4 = 2.93%. That is in line with the gap between Indian and US interest rates, so the quote looks fair.

children.text: Premium or Discount? It Depends on Who Pays More Interest

The rule is simple: the currency with the lower interest rate trades at a forward premium, and the currency with the higher interest rate trades at a forward discount. In USD/INR, the dollar has the lower rate, so the dollar is at a premium and USD/INR forwards sit above spot. In USD/JPY, Japanese rates are far lower than US rates, so the yen is at a premium and USD/JPY forwards sit below spot. The dollar is the same currency in both pairs, yet it is at a premium against the rupee and at a discount against the yen.

body.title: Above or below spot?
body.question: US interest rates are around 3.6% and Japanese interest rates are much lower. Where will the one-year USD/JPY forward rate be compared with spot?
options: Above spot, because the dollar is the stronger currency
Below spot, because the dollar has the higher interest rate
It depends on whether traders expect the yen to rise
body.explanation: The higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount. The dollar pays more interest than the yen, so fewer yen are needed per dollar for future delivery, and the USD/JPY forward sits below spot. Expectations do not set the forward. Interest rates do.

body.text: The forward premium is not a forecast of where the rupee will be. A 1-year forward at 98.17 does not mean the market expects USD/INR at 98.17 in a year. The rupee could end the year at 92 or at 102. The forward only reflects what it costs to lock a rate today. Anyone who says "forwards show the rupee will fall 2.8%" has misunderstood the arithmetic.

children.text: Forwards vs Futures

columns.label: OTC forward with a bank
points: Any amount and any date you agree with the bank
Actual dollars usually delivered at maturity
Profit or loss realised only at maturity
You depend on the bank honouring the contract
Used mainly by importers, exporters and borrowers to hedge real exposures

columns.label: USD/INR futures on NSE or BSE
points: Standard $1,000 lots with fixed monthly expiries
Cash-settled in rupees against the reference rate
Gains and losses settled every day through mark-to-market
Available through SEBI-registered brokers, but only to hedge a genuine currency exposure

markDefs.definition: Settling gains and losses on a futures position every day at that day's settlement price, so losses cannot pile up unpaid.

children.text: Because futures and forwards on the same date carry the same interest rate logic, the near-month NSE contract trades close to the one-month forward. That is why Chapter 2's second lesson showed futures at about 95.72 while spot was 95.50. The biggest practical difference for you is
mark-to-market
: if a futures position moves against you, your broker debits the loss that same evening, and you must keep enough margin in your account.

body.caption: Long USD/INR futures bought at 95.72. Every ₹1 rise in USD/INR gains ₹1,000 per $1,000 lot; every ₹1 fall loses the same. Unlike an option, there is no premium and no cap on the loss.

body.title: Daily settlement
body.textWithBlank: Futures gains and losses are settled every trading day through a process called ___.
body.explanation: Mark-to-market settles profits and losses daily at the settlement price, which is why exchange-traded futures need margin and why losses show up in your account immediately rather than at expiry.

children.text: Who Wins and Who Pays: Exporters vs Importers

The same premium helps one and costs the other. For an Indian exporter, the forward premium is a bonus earned for hedging. For an Indian importer, it is the price of certainty. Neither of them is guessing where the rupee will go. They are both removing the risk that it moves against them.

body.title: To hedge or not to hedge
body.scenario: Anita imports CNC machines into Rajkot and must pay a German supplier's US dollar invoice of $200,000 in three months. Spot is 95.50 and the 3-month forward is 96.19. Her cousin says: "Don't book a forward, you'll pay ₹1,38,000 extra for nothing. Just buy dollars on the day." Crude oil has been rising and FPIs have been selling Indian shares.
body.prompt: Evaluate her cousin's advice. What happens under each choice if USD/INR is 94.50 or 98.00 in three months, and how should Anita think about the decision?
body.modelAnswer:
1. If she hedges at 96.19, she pays ₹1,92,38,000 no matter what happens.
2. If she does not hedge and USD/INR is 94.50, she pays ₹1,89,00,000, saving ₹3,38,000 compared with the forward.
3. If she does not hedge and USD/INR is 98.00, she pays ₹1,96,00,000, which is ₹3,62,000 more than the forward.
4. The ₹1,38,000 is not wasted. It is the known cost of removing an unknown risk in either direction. Her cousin is really suggesting she speculate on the rupee with her business margin.
5. Rising crude and FPI selling add dollar demand, but that does not make a rupee fall certain. The right question is how much a ₹3 to ₹4 lakh swing would hurt her profit margin on this order. If it could wipe out her margin, hedging, fully or partly, is the disciplined choice.

cards.definition: A rate agreed today for exchanging currency on a future date, usually with a bank.
The amount by which the forward rate exceeds spot. In USD/INR it exists because Indian interest rates are higher than US rates.
F = S × (1 + r_INR × t) ÷ (1 + r_USD × t). Arbitrage keeps forwards in line with interest rate gaps.
The forward premium or discount quoted in paise, added to or subtracted from spot.
When the forward is below spot. The higher-interest currency trades at a forward discount.
Daily settlement of futures gains and losses at the exchange's settlement price.

points: Spot, forward and futures rates are prices for the same dollar delivered at different times.
USD/INR forwards sit above spot because Indian interest rates are higher than US rates. Arbitrage forces the forward to cancel out the interest gap.
The annual forward premium is roughly the Indian rate minus the US rate. It was about 2.8% for one year in mid-2026.
Forward points are quoted in paise. Annualise any premium with (F minus S) ÷ S × 12 ÷ months.
The lower-interest currency trades at a forward premium, the higher-interest currency at a discount.
A forward rate is not a forecast of the future spot rate.
Futures on NSE and BSE work like standardised forwards but are cash-settled, marked to market daily and guaranteed by a clearing corporation.
The forward premium benefits Indian exporters who hedge and is a cost for importers who hedge.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, trading or hedging advice. Interest rates, forward rates and scenarios used in the worked examples are illustrative. Policy rates and the forward premium shown are as of the dates stated and change frequently. Businesses should discuss hedging decisions with their bank and a qualified adviser.
